The adventure bike has become the default UK tourer, and it deserves the crown. Tall, comfortable, torquey and endlessly practical, a good ADV will carry you and a pillion round the NC500 in the morning and up a rutted forestry track in the afternoon without breaking stride. But there is a difference between owning an adventure bike and actually touring well on one. Here is how I set mine up and ride it after years of doing exactly this.

The adventure bike advantage

The upright riding position is the headline. Bars where your hands naturally fall, a commanding view over hedges and traffic, and a big-diameter front wheel that shrugs off potholes and gravel. On the Bealach na Ba, where the surface is patchy and the hairpins are steep, that geometry gives you confidence that a low sportbike simply cannot. Machines like the BMW R 1250 GS, the Honda Transalp XL750 and the KTM 890 Adventure all deliver this in slightly different flavours, from plush shaft-drive touring to sharp, rally-bred agility.

Luggage: hard, soft, or both

Adventure bikes are designed to carry luggage, so you have the widest choice of any category. The question is how far off-road you actually go.

  • Mostly tarmac touring: hard panniers win. A set of SW-Motech Trax Panniers are secure, weatherproof and double as a seat at the campsite.
  • Serious green-laning or gravel: soft luggage is safer and cheaper to damage. A Kriega OS-32 Adventure Pack will not trap your leg in a spill and packs down when empty.

Whatever you choose, respect the payload. It is easy to load an ADV like a transit van and then wonder why it wallows. Keep the heavy items low, use the panniers for weight and the top box for light, bulky things. Our luggage mounting guide covers rack fitment and weight distribution properly.

Wind protection and screens

Big adventure bikes usually come with adjustable screens, and getting yours dialled in is worth an afternoon of experimentation. Too low and you get chest blast; too high and you can get a helmet-buffeting turbulent zone. Aim for clean air just below your line of sight. If the stock screen fights you, an aftermarket touring screen or a bolt-on spoiler usually solves buffeting. For a full breakdown of shapes and sizing, see our motorcycle windscreen guide.

Handguards do double duty on an ADV, deflecting wind and rain off your hands and protecting the levers in a drop. I would not tour without a set of Barkbusters Handguards, and paired with Oxford Heated Grips they make grim Pennine mornings genuinely tolerable.

Comfort and ergonomics

The riding triangle is roomy, which suits long days and taller riders. Most ADVs have adjustable levers and often adjustable bars and seats. Spend time getting the seat height and bar reach right before a big trip, not on day one of it. Cruise control, where fitted, is a gift on long A-road hauls. If your seat is on the firm side, address it early; the miles an adventure bike can rack up will find any weakness in the padding.

An adventure bike will happily do 400 miles in a day. Whether you can is down to how well you have set up the contact points: seat, bars, pegs and screen.

Range and fuel strategy

This is a real strength. Most large ADVs carry 18-23 litres and return 50-60mpg on a touring run, so 200-plus miles between fills is normal and some will clear 250. That transforms Highland touring, where fuel stops are sparse. Even so, I plan around the tank, not my bladder: on remote stretches of the NC500 or the wilds beyond Ullapool I fill at every reliable station in the afternoon. Adventure bikes tempt you to explore side roads, and an empty tank 30 miles up a single-track glen is a long push.

Pace and riding the ADV well

An adventure bike flatters your pace. The torque means you rarely need to change down for an overtake, the suspension travel soaks up broken surfaces, and the wide bars give huge leverage through the A5 in Snowdonia or over the Cat and Fiddle. Use that composure rather than chasing outright speed. The magic of an ADV is covering big distances in comfort and then still having the ability to turn off the tarmac when a track catches your eye. A Cardo Packtalk Edge Intercom is worth its weight if you tour in a group or two-up, keeping everyone together and the navigation prompts flowing.

What to upgrade first

  • Handguards and heated grips.
  • Luggage matched to your riding style.
  • Screen fine-tuning or an aftermarket unit.
  • Crash protection (bars and bash plate) if you go off-road.
  • Tyres chosen for your tarmac-to-trail ratio.

Honest limitations

Big adventure bikes are heavy, and a 250kg machine with full luggage is a handful in a tight car park or when you drop it two hours from anywhere. Seat heights can be intimidating for shorter riders. Genuine off-road ability on the largest models is limited by that weight, whatever the marketing says; the mid-size Transalp and 890 Adventure are far more willing in the dirt than the biggest flagships. And fuel economy suffers if you ride the torque hard.

Who it suits

Adventure bikes suit riders who want one bike to do everything: commute, tour two-up, and occasionally leave the tarmac. They reward taller riders and anyone who values an upright view and all-day comfort. If you are still choosing, our roundup of the best touring bikes for 2026 puts the leading ADVs head to head. Set one up properly and there is genuinely no UK road, or lack of road, it cannot handle.

Large ADVs carry 18-23 litres and return 50-60mpg, so 200-plus miles between fills is normal.
The biggest models are heavy off-road, so mid-size ADVs are more willing in the dirt.

faq.q: Why are adventure bikes so popular for UK touring?
faq.a: The upright riding position is the headline: bars where your hands naturally fall, a commanding view over hedges and traffic, and a big front wheel that shrugs off potholes and gravel. On patchy, steep roads like Bealach na Ba, that geometry gives confidence a low sportbike cannot. Add excellent range, comfort and the ability to leave the tarmac, and the ADV genuinely earns its place as the default tourer.

faq.q: Should I fit hard or soft luggage to an ADV?
faq.a: It depends how far off-road you go. For mostly-tarmac touring, hard panniers win, being secure, weatherproof and doubling as a campsite seat. For serious green-laning or gravel, soft luggage is safer in a spill and cheaper to damage, and it will not trap your leg. Whatever you choose, respect the payload and keep heavy items low, using panniers for weight and the top box for light, bulky things.

faq.q: How far can an adventure bike go on a tank?
faq.a: Range is a real strength. Most large ADVs carry 18 to 23 litres and return 50 to 60mpg on a touring run, so 200-plus miles between fills is normal and some clear 250. That transforms Highland touring where fuel is sparse. Even so, plan around the tank rather than your bladder and fill at every reliable station in remote country, as an empty tank up a single-track glen is a long push.

faq.q: Can big adventure bikes actually go off-road?
faq.a: Up to a point. The upright geometry and long-travel suspension handle broken surfaces and green lanes well, but genuine off-road ability on the largest 250kg-plus flagships is limited by weight, whatever the marketing says. Mid-size machines like the Honda Transalp and KTM 890 Adventure are far more willing in the dirt. Fit crash protection and appropriate tyres if you plan to leave the tarmac regularly.
